idiom_name: catch (SpecificException) { } with a named or omitted variable, or `_ =` on a fire-and-forget Task
implementation_notes: C# does not force handling, so the mute is written by hand: a catch clause for one narrow exception type with an empty body, the caught variable omitted or named `ignored`, plus a comment that states why. For asynchronous fire-and-forget the same intent takes the form of an explicit discard, `_ = SomeAsync();`, which documents that the task is deliberately not awaited. Where the BCL offers a non-failing API, use it instead (int.TryParse, Dictionary.TryGetValue, File.Delete, which reports nothing) - the classic empty catch is justified only for framework or third-party calls that signal expected conditions as exceptions.
pitfalls: Analyzer rules (CA1031 'Do not catch general exception types', SonarQube's empty-block rules, IDE0059-style findings) flag mutes, so an unexplained empty catch breaks the build or gets disabled project-wide - keep the mute narrow and commented.

`catch (Exception) { }` around a Task swallows the AggregateException semantics: the failure never surfaces, not even in logs, because unobserved-fault reporting (TaskScheduler.UnobservedTaskException) only sees faults that were never awaited or observed at all.

An un-annotated `_ = Task` discard hides the difference between 'cancelled during shutdown' and 'broken': muting an OperationCanceledException alongside a real fault makes the two indistinguishable in production.
